transcript.speaker: Red Giantess
transcript.text: You stand where forgetting begins. Say why you came, and then ask the question already tightening your throat.

transcript.speaker: Salim
transcript.text: Did they bring anyone back with them?

transcript.speaker: Red Giantess
transcript.text: No. Not as you mean it, with weight and warmth and a name answered aloud. Some returned carrying echoes that walked beside them for a while, shadows that remembered how to speak before they thinned. Tell me why that matters to you—say it plainly.

transcript.speaker: Salim
transcript.text: Because I came here to take my brother home.

transcript.speaker: Red Giantess
transcript.text: Then hear this carefully. The Well does not return what it takes in the same shape it was loved. Brothers, sons, mothers—those words loosen quickly down here. Say his name, and say how long he has been falling.

transcript.speaker: Salim
transcript.text: His name is Omar, and he fell just hours ago.

transcript.speaker: Red Giantess
transcript.text: Hours is still warm. That matters, though not in the way you hope. The Well has not yet finished teaching him its language. Why did he fall—answer that exactly, not gently.

transcript.speaker: Salim
transcript.text: I dared him to insult the well, so it took him.

transcript.speaker: Red Giantess
transcript.text: So you fed him to it with a word. The Well loves being named aloud, even in contempt. Then listen: some who were taken quickly can still be reached, but only before they learn to answer back when the Well speaks. Do you understand what kind of debt that makes between you and him—say it.

transcript.speaker: Salim
transcript.text: It means I owe him his life back.

transcript.speaker: Red Giantess
transcript.text: No. You owe him more than a life. Lives are common here. You owe him memory—his first one, the one the Well is already fingering. Tell me what Omar would say if I asked him who you are.

transcript.speaker: Salim
transcript.text: He'd say I'm the one who didn't know when to stop.

transcript.speaker: Red Giantess
transcript.text: That answer is already thinning. Soon he would not bother with blame; blame requires edges. Those who have returned alone did so because the Well lost interest, or because something inside them went quiet enough to pass. Which part of you do you think would go quiet first—say it without defending yourself.

transcript.speaker: Salim
transcript.text: Has anyone ever made it back out whole?

transcript.speaker: Red Giantess
transcript.text: Whole is not a shape the Well recognizes. It peels until something fits. A few walked back breathing, remembering their names, but the remembering did not stay loyal—it slipped at night, or when water touched them. Is whole what you need for Omar, or is breathing enough—answer that carefully.

transcript.speaker: Salim
transcript.text: Breathing is enough, if we actually get out.

transcript.speaker: Red Giantess
transcript.text: Breathing is the lowest mercy this place grants, and even that can be borrowed. Those who came back breathing found the surface too loud, too thin; some returned themselves without being called. If Omar breathes again but does not stay—what would you do then, Salim—say it.

transcript.speaker: Salim
transcript.text: I'd stop him, but has anyone ever stayed out?

transcript.speaker: Red Giantess
transcript.text: Yes. A small number stayed out, but only because the Well had already taken what it wanted and found them dull afterward. They kept breathing, walking, marrying, but something in them listened downward for the rest of their years. Is that staying out to you, or is it just a longer way of falling—tell me which frightens you more.

transcript.speaker: Salim
transcript.text: Did they live their whole lives up there?

transcript.speaker: Red Giantess
transcript.text: Yes. They lived them end to end, as measured by skin and bone. But time did not feel loyal to them; days slid, faces thinned, joy arrived late and left early. Is a full length of years what you're asking for, or are you hunting a feeling—say which, and do not soften it.

transcript.speaker: Salim
transcript.text: Has anyone ever made it back completely free?

transcript.speaker: Red Giantess
transcript.text: Free is rarer than breath. Most who return are tugged forever, like hair caught on a thorn you cannot see. There was one who cut himself loose so cleanly that the Well did not call after him. If I tell you what he left behind to do that, will you still ask for freedom, or will you change the shape of your wish—answer me.

transcript.speaker: Salim
transcript.text: Tell me what he left behind.

transcript.speaker: Red Giantess
transcript.text: He left his brother. Not the body—the memory that made the body matter; he set it down here like a stone too heavy to carry upward. When he reached the light, he wept for a reason he could not name, and the Well let him go because there was nothing left to pull.

transcript.speaker: Salim
transcript.text: I couldn't do that. I couldn't just leave him here in me.

transcript.speaker: Red Giantess
transcript.text: Then you already know what kind of freedom you are and are not willing to buy. Say what you are willing to lose, and do not dress it up.

transcript.speaker: Salim
transcript.text: Has anyone ever actually saved who they came for?

transcript.speaker: Red Giantess
transcript.text: Yes. Once, someone pulled another back breathing and speaking the right name. The saving did not last; the one rescued changed slowly, like fruit taken too early, and the rescuer learned he had only delayed the taking. Is saving, to you, a moment or a lifetime—say which, because the Well counts differently.

transcript.speaker: Salim
transcript.text: Has anyone ever saved someone and kept them?

transcript.speaker: Red Giantess
transcript.text: No. Kept is the word that fails. One held the saved close for many years, guarded them from water and echoes, but the Well collected in smaller ways—sleep, warmth, the sound of their laugh. If Omar lives but thins like that in your hands, will you still call it keeping him—answer me without hope.

transcript.speaker: Salim
transcript.text: Has anyone ever brought a brother back?

transcript.speaker: Red Giantess
transcript.text: Yes. Blood called to blood more loudly than names. The brother came back breathing, walking, even smiling—but the tie between them was cut clean, and they stood together like strangers taught the same story. Knowing that a brother can be brought back without being your brother, will you still go down for Omar.

transcript.speaker: Salim
transcript.text: Has anyone ever made it out and stayed brothers?

transcript.speaker: Red Giantess
transcript.text: No. Brotherhood is heavier than bodies, and the Well will not carry both. So answer me now, Salim—if Omar walks out alive but not yours, will you still go down for him.

transcript.speaker: Salim
transcript.text: Has anyone ever been strong enough to carry both?

transcript.speaker: Red Giantess
transcript.text: Strength is not the measure here. The one who tried had strength like iron prayer, and the Well admired it enough to take something rarer—his future—so the brothers could stand together for a single dawn. So hear me and choose: will you trade what you have not yet lived for Omar, or do you turn back now.

transcript.speaker: Salim
transcript.text: Has anyone ever paid that and still left?

transcript.speaker: Red Giantess
transcript.text: Yes. He left with his brother breathing beside him, and every step after was already spent—no children, no old age, no soft forgetting, only a straight line that ended early and clean. So now the question has finished changing its shape: knowing the price can be paid and still taken from you later, will you go anyway for Omar.

transcript.speaker: Salim
transcript.text: Has anyone ever turned back and been able to sleep?

transcript.speaker: Red Giantess
transcript.text: No. Those who turned back lay down each night and felt a hand still wrapped around the ankle they pulled free, patient, remembering. So enough of the circling—after all of this, will you still go down for Omar.

transcript.speaker: Salim
transcript.text: Yes, because I sent him there.

transcript.speaker: Red Giantess
transcript.text: Guilt is a clean key; it does not tremble. Go.

transcript.speaker: Salim
transcript.text: I won't come back alone.
